_README: Copy this file to add an application -- one joint on one robot. Put it in
applications/ (gitignored) rather than in here, which is public.
cp applications/examples/_TEMPLATE.json applications/my_elbow.json
./eval_actuator.py -a robstride_00 -j my_elbow --save --charts
Delete any field you do not need. Requirements you leave out are derived
from the motion profile instead. Do NOT invent numbers to fill gaps: an
omitted field gets a documented default and shows up in the report's
assumption list and sensitivity sweep, whereas a fabricated one looks like
data and silently corrupts the verdict.
UNITS. Every physical value may be written three ways:
1. explicit object   "distance_joint_axis_to_CG": {"value": 11, "units": "in"}  <- preferred
2. suffixed name     "distance_joint_axis_to_CG_mm": 280
3. bare number       "distance_joint_axis_to_CG": 0.28  -> canonical SI assumed, and
flagged with ! in the report's UNIT AUDIT
A unit from the wrong dimension (kg for a length) is always a hard error.
Set "strict_units": true to reject form 3 outright.
Canonical units: mass kg, length m, inertia kg.m^2, angle rad, time s,
EXCEPT joint angles (stroke_start, stroke_end, gravity_angle), where a bare
number is read as DEGREES -- nobody writes 90 meaning 90 radians.
torque N.m, angular velocity rad/s, temperature degC, voltage V.
MINIMUM VIABLE ENTRY: a name, a load, and either a profile or duty_segments.
Everything else has a defensible default.
name: My Elbow
_n_actuators: How many actuators share this joint in parallel. Torque and mass scale by n
and each unit carries 1/n of the load, so every unit's thermal problem gets
easier. Compare options with -n 1,2,3 on the command line rather than
_ratio: Extra reduction between the actuator OUTPUT and the joint itself -- a belt,
a linkage, a second gear stage. Leave at 1.0 for actuators mounted coaxially
on the joint axis. ratio_type sets the default efficiency and is one of:
direct | planetary_1stage | planetary_2stage | cycloidal | harmonic | belt | worm

ratio.note: actuator mounted coaxially on the joint, no extra reduction

_load: What the joint has to move. Describe the ENTIRE moving assembly as one rigid
body -- link, bracket, hardware, and anything it carries -- using the three
numbers every CAD system reports for it:
total_mass_at_CG            total mass of the moving portion
distance_joint_axis_to_CG   joint axis to the centre of gravity
moment_of_inertia_around_CG inertia about the CG, NOT about the joint axis
There is no separate 'payload': a head-tilt joint that carries nothing states
the head itself here, exactly as an elbow states link plus cargo combined.
This module refers them to the joint axis for you, by the parallel axis
theorem, and that is the whole point -- you never state anything about the
joint axis, so nothing can be double-counted:
INERTIA  (resists acceleration) = moment_of_inertia_around_CG
+ total_mass_at_CG*distance_joint_axis_to_CG^2
GRAVITY  (resists holding)      = total_mass_at_CG*g*distance_joint_axis_to_CG
* cos(joint_plane_tilt)
* sin(theta - gravity_angle)
If all you have is an inertia about the JOINT AXIS, subtract the transfer
term first: moment_of_inertia_around_CG = I_axis - m*d^2. Quoting an
axis-referred figure directly counts m*d^2 twice.
Note distance_joint_axis_to_CG counts twice over: linearly for gravity,
SQUARED for inertia. It is the input most worth getting right.
Only the CG OFFSET produces gravity torque; inertia about the CG never does.
BOTH gravity fields are referenced to the GRAVITY VECTOR, as in standard
mechanics -- you state how the joint sits relative to gravity, not where
gravity happens to bite hardest.
gravity_angle: the joint angle at which the CG points straight DOWN,
along gravity. It hangs there, so torque is ZERO at gravity_angle and peaks
90 deg away. Same angle frame as profile.stroke_start / stroke_end.
joint_plane_tilt: side-side tilt of this joint's plane of rotation relative
to gravity. 0 = the plane is vertical and contains the gravity vector, so
gravity acts fully (an elbow or pitch joint). 90 deg = the plane is
horizontal and the axis is vertical, so gravity exerts no torque at any
angle (a pan or yaw joint). This is NOT expressible as an angle offset:
no value of gravity_angle can flatten the cosine, only the tilt can.
Both describe how the joint is MOUNTED and cannot be derived from the motion.
_profile: A repeated point-to-point move, stated the way a motion controller states
it: the two endpoints plus the three KINEMATIC limits the controller
enforces. The tool then generates the fastest S-curve that respects all
three and builds the whole torque/speed/time history from it, including
inertia, gravity and the reflected rotor inertia of the actuators fitted.
Because the limits are the input, MOVE TIME IS AN OUTPUT. There is no
move_time or accel_fraction field: prescribing a duration and asking whether
the actuator can meet it is the old way round. Now you state the limits your
robot actually runs, and the report tells you the resulting move time, which
limit binds, and whether the actuator can follow it.
stroke_start and stroke_end are joint angles in the SAME frame as
load.gravity_angle, so where the move sits relative to gravity is explicit.
Both default to degrees if you write a bare number. Order is free: defining
the move end-to-start simply runs it the other way.
max_velocity  joint speed ceiling. Reached only if the stroke is long
enough; when it is, the move gets a constant-speed cruise.
max_accel     acceleration ceiling. KINEMATIC, not a torque limit -- the
torque it demands is J_total*max_accel, computed for you.
max_jerk      how fast acceleration may change, so there are no
instantaneous torque steps. Lower is gentler but slower.
dwell_time    rest at EACH end, after arriving and before returning.
One full cycle is 2*(solved move_time + dwell_time). Whichever limit binds
sets the shape, and the report names it:
velocity-limited  7 phases, a cruise exists (long stroke)
accel-limited     6 phases, hits max_accel but never max_velocity
jerk-limited      4 phases, so short it never even reaches max_accel
Chart 1 legend maps straight onto these:
Move_*_Accel / Move_*_Decel   the ramps
Cruise                        the constant-velocity part, if any
Dwell                         dwell_time
max_accel is the sizing knob: torque scales with it directly, so doubling it
doubles the inertial torque demand. If your controller limits TORQUE rather
than acceleration, the report's COMMANDED MOTION block gives 'implied
inertial torq' = J_total * peak accel, at the joint and per actuator output:
adjust max_accel until that matches your controller's cap. Two cautions --
it is the acceleration actually COMMANDED, which equals max_accel only when
the line above reads AT LIMIT (a short stroke may be jerk-limited and never
get there), and it is the INERTIAL term alone, so gravity, friction and
external torque are extra. If your cap covers total torque instead, compare
against the DUTY CYCLE peak torque demand.
dwell_time is the main knob over heating
-- the charts sweep it. samples only sets time resolution: more segments,
more dots on chart 1, a slightly better RMS. It does not change the motion.
If you already have a measured torque/speed history, delete this block and
use duty_segments below instead.
_duty_segments: Alternative to profile: an explicit [[dt, torque, speed], ...] history at the
JOINT, with the units declared alongside. Takes precedence over profile if
both are present. Include the rest periods as zero-speed segments -- and note
that a gravity-loaded joint still draws holding current at zero speed.
_POWER_SYSTEM: Bus voltage is a property of THIS robot, not of the actuator. The vendor's
rated voltage is only what they characterised the unit at. Set the voltage
your robot actually supplies here; the actuator file declares the range it
will accept, and the two are checked against each other.
Running ABOVE the vendor nominal is routine and simply extends the speed
envelope -- higher voltage buys speed, not torque and not thermal margin.
Running above their stated MAXIMUM is limited by transistor and DC-link
capacitor ratings rather than by heat, so it cannot be cleared on thermal
grounds; set accept_overvoltage true to acknowledge the risk and downgrade
that check from a failure to a warning.
Omit bus_voltage entirely to fall back to the actuator's nominal.
supply_current_limit is optional -- omit it if the supply can always deliver
more than the drive's own current rating, which is the usual case.

bus_voltage.note: state the pack you actually use, e.g. 13S lithium

_THERMAL: T_ambient is the air INSIDE your shell next to the actuator, not room
temperature. It is routinely 15-25 degC above ambient in an enclosed arm and
it moves the thermal verdict more than almost anything else.
max_surface_temp turns the computed housing temperature into a pass/fail
criterion, and is frequently the real constraint on a human-adjacent robot.
ISO 13732-1 is the relevant standard for touch limits; the threshold depends
on material and contact duration, so set it from your own safety case. Omit
it if the housing is not reachable by an operator.
mounting sets the default case-to-ambient thermal resistance and is one of:

T_ambient.note: inside the arm shell, NOT room temperature

max_surface_temp.note: housing reachable by the operator; set from your own safety case

_REQUIREMENTS: Optional hard requirements. Anything omitted is derived from the motion
above, so only set these where you have a real specification to meet: they
are combined with the computed demand using whichever is larger.
require_backdrivable adds a check that the joint can be pushed by hand,
_OPTIONAL_REQUIREMENTS: "lead": {"value": 5, "units": "mm"}   <- prismatic joints: m per output rev
